analysis.one_liner: Bans most large mergers and buyouts for the duration of the COVID-19 emergency.
analysis.headline: The bill never left committee: it was referred to the House Judiciary Committee on May 22, 2020 and received no further action before the 116th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have frozen most mergers and acquisitions while the COVID-19 emergency was underway. It barred companies with more than $100 million in revenue, big banks and private equity funds, and owners of COVID-related patents from buying other firms, unless they won a waiver by showing the deal served national security or public health. It also set up a lasting presumption against any deal that could weaken the government's ability to respond to a future emergency, and hit violators with a penalty of at least 10% of their annual revenue.
analysis.who_benefits: Small businesses and their workers, who during a pandemic-driven downturn are often sold cheaply to large competitors or private equity buyers; the moratorium aimed to keep those businesses independent and employers intact while markets were depressed.

how_it_helps.text: During the COVID-19 emergency, the bill prohibited acquisitions by firms with over $100 million in revenue and by financial institutions or equity funds with over $100 million in capitalization, so that large buyers could not pick off weakened competitors while markets were depressed.

It blocked acquisitions involving firms holding exclusive patents on COVID-19-related production, manufacturing, distribution, medical supplies, equipment, and drug research, production, and distribution.

It created a legal presumption against any transaction that could reduce the government's ability to produce, procure, or stockpile life-saving goods and services during the pandemic or other emergencies, and put the burden on firms to prove otherwise.
Firms attempting a prohibited deal faced an order blocking or reversing the transaction plus a penalty of at least 10% of their fiscal year 2019 revenue.

The moratorium would not have ended until the FTC unanimously voted, only after the national emergency ended, every state had reopened, and the FTC determined small businesses and workers were no longer under severe financial distress.

analysis.who_pays: Large corporations, banks, private equity funds, and patent-holding drug and medical supply companies that would have been barred from buying competitors or distressed firms until the emergency had fully passed; some dealmakers argue the freeze would also have slowed capital reaching struggling companies, though a failing-firm waiver and a national-interest waiver were available.
analysis.who_pays_short: Big acquirers, private equity, and patent holders

drawbacks.text: The ban was sweeping: it covered any acquisition reportable under the Clayton Act, effectively pausing nearly all significant M&A nationwide during the pandemic, which defenders of dealmaking said would freeze legitimate transactions and capital-raising, not just predatory ones.

Ending the moratorium required a unanimous FTC vote plus agreement from several cabinet secretaries, and could happen only after every state had reopened its economy and the FTC found small businesses and workers no longer under severe distress — conditions that could have kept the freeze in place long after the acute crisis.

The penalty — at least 10% of a firm's fiscal 2019 revenue — is unusually large by antitrust standards and, combined with orders reversing completed deals, would have exposed ordinary shareholders and employees of violators to major costs.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targeted a real and well-documented pattern: in downturns, distressed small businesses sell cheaply to large competitors and private equity, which can leave communities with fewer employers and consumers with less competition. Its failing-firm waiver and national-interest waiver were designed to let rescue transactions through. The honest objections are that the ban was far broader than predatory buyouts alone, the sunset conditions were hard to meet, and the revenue-based penalty was harsh; a narrower moratorium would have balanced those concerns better. But as written, the main beneficiaries were workers and small firms, and the main costs fell on large acquirers.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up before the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez introduced the bill on May 22, 2020, with Reps. Jesús García and Ilhan Omar as the only cosponsors, and it was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary.
No further action was ever recorded on the bill; it stayed in the Judiciary Committee until the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021, and it never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large acquirers, private equity funds, and holders of COVID-related patents were better off, because no moratorium ever took effect and they remained free to buy competitors and distressed companies throughout the pandemic downturn.

for.name: Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the House Judiciary Committee on May 22, 2020.

for.name: Rep. Jesús "Chuy" García
for.what_they_did: Joined as an original cosponsor at introduction.

for.name: Rep. Ilhan Omar
for.what_they_did: Joined as an original cosponsor at introduction.

against.name: Rep. Jerrold Nadler
against.role: Chair, House Committee on the Judiciary
against.what_they_did: The Judiciary Committee, which he chaired, never scheduled the bill for a hearing or markup in the roughly seven months it had remaining, leaving it to die in committee.

sides.party_line_note: All three sponsors were House Democrats and no Republican signed on, but the bill also never advanced in the Democrat-controlled Judiciary Committee, so the opposition that mattered was inaction by the majority itself.

industries.industry: Large acquirers (firms with over $100 million in revenue)
industries.note: The bill barred these firms from any acquisitions during the COVID-19 emergency unless they won a waiver. Their gain would have come at the price of weakened small businesses and competitors being absorbed at depressed pandemic prices.

industries.industry: Private equity funds and financial institutions
industries.note: Funds and institutions with over $100 million in capitalization, plus registered investment advisers, could not buy companies during the moratorium. Distressed buyouts during downturns are a core private equity strategy, and the bill would have paused it.

industries.industry: Pharmaceutical, medical supply, and device patent holders
industries.note: Acquisitions involving firms with exclusive patents on COVID-related production, supplies, and drug development were prohibited. This kept control of pandemic-relevant products out of consolidation while the emergency was underway.
